target: AG1's claim that AI is broadly good for society because it improves convenience, health, safety, productivity, accessibility, and opportunity
objection: AI is not good for society overall because its widespread adoption tends to erode economic security, weaken critical thinking, intensify racial bias, and create serious privacy risks.

target: AG1's assumption that AI-driven automation mainly augments workers and can be offset by retraining and retention efforts
objection: Even when AI automates routine work, it often displaces workers faster than it creates new opportunities, and companies have strong incentives to cut costs rather than invest in retraining, so AI harms labor stability rather than reliably improving it.

target: AG1's claim that AI can support learning by helping students and professionals focus on higher-value work
objection: AI tools can replace practice and judgment, causing students and adults to rely on generated answers instead of building the skills needed to evaluate evidence and reason independently.

target: AG1's claim that AI can be made fair through responsible use
objection: AI systems can reproduce and amplify racial stereotypes because they learn from biased data and then reflect biased outcomes back into the world, so they can worsen racial inequity.

target: AG1's claim that privacy risks are manageable with responsible deployment
objection: AI frequently requires large-scale data collection and can infer sensitive traits about people, creating serious risks of surveillance and misuse.

target: AG1's claim that the main harms of AI are not inevitable and can be solved through design and governance
objection: In real-world adoption, AI harms are structurally hard to prevent because business incentives favor speed and cost reduction over worker stability, making mitigation unreliable.

target: AG1's claim that AI can function as an educational coach that improves critical thinking
objection: Even when framed as a coach, most users will still use AI as an answer source under time pressure, which changes study habits and reduces verification and reasoning practice.

target: AG1's claim that fairness testing and audits can substantially reduce racial bias in AI systems
objection: Audits and fairness tests do not fully solve bias because models can behave opaquely, bias can re-enter through new data and deployment contexts, and minorities can still receive systematically worse outcomes.

target: AG1's claim that privacy risks can be reduced through data minimization, consent controls, and other privacy-preserving techniques
objection: Those privacy safeguards are often not the default in commercial AI, and even privacy-preserving methods can be undermined by large-scale data collection and inference from non-sensitive inputs.

target: AG1's claim that policy guardrails can make AI net positive
objection: Enforceable AI rules do not scale well to fast-changing deployment, and compliance often becomes performative or is undermined by regulatory gaps, cross-border deployment, and corporate lobbying, so safety rules are not reliably effective.

target: AG1's claim that AI benefits and harms can be balanced through transition support and gain-sharing
objection: Even when AI raises productivity, the gains tend to accrue to large firms and model owners while workers and small businesses absorb the shocks, so transition support often fails to reach the people harmed by automation.

target: AG1's claim that privacy standards and consent can control AI-related data harms
objection: At scale, AI encourages pervasive collection and inference, including behavioral profiling and surveillance-like systems, which disproportionately expose minorities to scrutiny and leave them with less recourse.

target: AG1's claim that targeted deployment can keep AI beneficial while restricting harmful uses
objection: Once AI infrastructure is adopted, it tends to spill over into other domains because it is profitable and easy to repurpose, so targeted deployment is not a durable guarantee against broader harm.

target: AG1's claim that automation bias can be mitigated through citations, uncertainty labels, and traceable reasoning
objection: Critical thinking erosion is hard to prevent because users under time pressure internalize AI outputs as authority anyway, so training and policy do not reliably stop shortcut behavior.

target: AG1's claim that AI can help counter misinformation and manipulation through provenance and detection tools
objection: AI also greatly expands persuasive text, audio, and video generation, which increases misinformation, polarization, and manipulation in ways that cannot be fully contained by per-application testing.

target: AG1's claim that restricted AI systems and auditing can prevent harmful spillover
objection: Provenance and detection are a cat-and-mouse game because attackers can spoof, remix, or synthesize outputs to evade controls, leaving society in a constant arms race rather than stable protection.

target: AG1's claim that verification-centered design will preserve reasoning instead of replacing it
objection: Requiring citations, uncertainty displays, and show-your-work features shifts the burden onto users, who often lack the time or expertise to verify outputs and will still treat AI as authoritative.

target: AG1's claim that AI-based monitoring and fact-checking can reduce manipulation without major downsides
objection: Safety auditing usually requires more data collection, logging, and monitoring, which intensifies privacy risks and can deepen surveillance-like pressures, especially for minorities.
